| `/jukeloop restart` | Manage Messages | Reconnect and restart JukeLoop without redeploying the bot. |

Wallet addresses submitted in Discord are community claims, not cryptographic proof of wallet ownership. During this manual bootstrap phase, the owner must verify unexpected or disputed addresses before approving a mint.

### MP4 Videos and CID Submissions

Discord audio and MP4 attachments are accepted up to and including 10 MB; larger attachments are rejected before playlist ingestion or IPFS pinning. Restart backfill also discovers older MP4 posts within that cap. Attachments enter the artist's `/jukebox backlog`, not the mint queue automatically: use `/jukebox request-mint` to supply the artist wallet, or have the owner run `/jukeloop queue-uploads uploader:<artist> wallet:<artist Base wallet>` for the full pinned backlog. FFmpeg extracts only the audio (`-vn`) for the JukeLoop Discord voice channel. DecentBusking plays the MP4 video above the NFT scene at 84% opacity, with the same synchronized position and radio mute/volume controls. The video button hides or shows the picture without creating a second audio stream. Use H.264 video with AAC audio for broad browser compatibility; silent videos have no voice-channel audio, and other MP4 codecs may not play in every browser.

For files over the 10 MB Discord attachment limit, pin the file to IPFS and use:

```text
/jukebox submit cid:<file CID> title:<title> wallet:<artist Base wallet> format:mp4
```

The CID must identify the media file itself, not an album directory or a gateway URL. The command queues owner approval without downloading or re-uploading the file. Existing `/jukebox request-mint` can add artwork to that request.

The site's briefcase supports audio/MP4 file uploads up to 50 MB, or an existing file CID for larger media. Artwork accepts PNG, JPEG, WebP, or GIF up to 10 MB. An artist signs the upload and submission with their connected wallet; this grants no on-chain mint permission. The submitted recipient must match that wallet unless the owner is submitting. Artist uploads are restricted to supported media/artwork, allowed site origins, fresh signatures, replay protection, and 20 upload/submission requests per wallet per hour. These limits are in memory and reset when the service restarts; monitor Pinata quotas for this public upload service.

Site submissions join the existing private owner mint queue. They remain outside radio rotation and new-upload previews until the owner mints and the verified transaction is reconciled. The owner Admin panel and CLI preserve video type, artwork, tip wallet, and parent-token lineage in NFT metadata. Neither a submission nor an upload sends a blockchain transaction. Redeploy the Render bot/worker and publish the static frontend together to enable these routes; no new environment variables are required.

Successful Discord media uploads still receive a **Request NFT** button after the
file is pinned. It embeds the Track ID automatically and opens a private
wallet/artwork form for the original uploader. A single previously used artist
wallet is prefilled for confirmation; otherwise the artist enters it. Artwork is
optional: attach PNG, JPEG, WebP, or GIF up to 10 MB, or enter an already-uploaded
IPFS image file CID for larger artwork. The CID field accepts a bare CID or
`ipfs://CID`, not directory paths or gateway URLs, and does not re-upload the
image or impose the Discord attachment-size cap. Choose one source, not both.

Leaving both fields blank keeps existing artwork or uses the Discord profile image
by default when no artwork exists. The bot explicitly reminds the artist of that
default and queues owner approval; it does not send a mint transaction. If the
profile image cannot be archived, the artist is asked to retry or supply artwork
rather than silently queuing an image-less NFT. Old confirmation messages do not
gain buttons automatically; `/jukebox request-mint` remains available for those
tracks and as a fallback.

`/jukebox request-mint` only queues a request; it does not submit a blockchain transaction. Artists may attach PNG, JPEG, WebP, or GIF artwork up to 10 MB; the bot pins it immediately and stores its CID with the request. The contract owner opens **Admin** in the DecentBusking dapp, uses the connected `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` wallet, and authorizes the private queue. Artist artwork is previewed and preloaded, with an optional replacement control. Each request has an individual Mint action. Multiple selected requests can be processed sequentially; the current contract has no batch registration method, so MetaMask still requires two Base transaction confirmations per track. The browser reports each confirmed mint to the Render worker. After the worker verifies the owner, contract, recipient, token ID, and `EditionMinted` event on Base, the bot removes the item from the backlog and announces the NFT in both configured public text channels. `/jukeloop mint-queue` and `/jukeloop mark-minted` remain recovery tools.

A true one-confirmation batch is possible through a separately deployed `BatchProductMinter` helper contract holding `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`: it can loop over requests and use each `registerToken` return value immediately in `mintProduct`. That privileged helper requires its own Solidity project, review, deployment, and explicit role grant before the dapp should use it.

Admin reuses the wallet connected in the site header; opening the panel checks the on-chain admin role without another connection request or message signature. NFT Requests starts collapsed: expanding it loads the private queue and requests its owner-wallet message signature, since a public address alone is not proof of ownership. Closing that section does not sign. That authorization is reused in memory for four minutes (within the worker's five-minute validity window), then refreshed when needed. It is cleared on account/network changes or disconnect and never stored in browser storage. Upload authorizations and on-chain mint transactions remain separate approvals.

The Admin sections appear in this order: Radio Programming, NFT Requests, Live
Performance, DVert, Worker funding, Contract Roles. The connected wallet reuses
the creator-profile four-icon identity label, with `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` beside it
below the header divider. Balance warnings and verified Base funding details stay
inside Worker funding; a low balance does not force the section open and never
initiates a transfer. The balance, threshold and runway remain live readings, not
hardcoded display values.

## JukeLoop — 24/7 Community Radio

JukeLoop automatically streams every audio file posted in `#DecentJukebox` to the `JukeLoop` voice channel, non-stop.

### How it works

```
Bot starts up
    ↓

Loads playlist from jukeloop-playlist.json (persisted across restarts)
    ↓
Scans ALL historic messages in #DecentJukebox for audio attachments (backfill)
    ↓
Joins the JukeLoop voice channel
    ↓
Builds a weighted-random playlist (higher-rated tracks play sooner/more often)
    ↓
Plays each track and announces it with a website link and reminder to vote there
    ↓
When the next track starts, reads the reaction counts and updates ratings
    ↓
After each full loop, reshuffles using fresh weights → repeat forever
```

### Rating system

| Reaction | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| 👍 | +1 to the track's score |
| 👎 | −0.5 to the track's score |

Track weight = `max(0.1, 1 + likes − dislikes × 0.5)`.  A brand-new track has weight 1.0.  Higher weight = higher probability of appearing earlier in each loop pass.  Even heavily down-voted tracks still appear occasionally (weight floor: 0.1).

Ratings **accumulate** across plays and **persist to disk** (`jukeloop-playlist.json`) so they survive bot restarts.

The playlist is the single master tally. The local runtime file and tagged Pinata snapshots are copies of that ledger, not independent vote lists. Both Playback Tally panels read its counters; the personal panel filters by the artist wallet.

Site votes, Now Playing reactions, and reactions on an original upload that identifies exactly one track update the same track totals. Discord reaction additions/removals are synchronized live; each message has a persisted count baseline, so rereading it adds only the difference. Thumb skin-tone variants count, and the bot's own seed reactions do not. Reactions remain available after a play finishes. Multi-track upload posts are not assigned a vote arbitrarily; listeners can react on each track's Now Playing message instead.

New JukeLoop and AdLoop announcements do not seed thumb reactions: they link to
`SITE_URL` and direct listeners to vote on the website. Posting an announcement now
uses one REST request instead of a message plus two reaction requests, a two-thirds
reduction for announcement creation, not for all bot traffic. Existing/manual
Discord reactions still synchronize, and historical rating recovery is unchanged.

On startup, JukeLoop scans up to 500 recent announcements and checkpoints recovered changes. For older messages, readable reactions and bot-published cumulative counters establish a one-time conservative minimum; those two representations are not added together. Reactions erased by older bot versions cannot be reconstructed. New announcements carry a Play ID, and completed audible plays retain their announcement ID, preventing recovery from adding the same play twice. Historical totals do not create qualified weekly playback credits.

Playback payroll uses qualified plays (completed Discord audio with at least 30 audible seconds) and verified artist wallets. New payout buckets close Monday 00:00 `America/New_York`, retain legacy UTC history and lifetime totals, and start with a labelled partial migration week. Top 10 prizes use live weekly net-vote buckets, not historic/all-time totals. Site votes are anonymous; prize recipients still require owner review.

`GET /api/payroll/weekly` exposes the current New York period, closing time, funding/commitments, warnings and published closed-week receipts; `?wallet=0x...` filters provisional artist/song shares. The running worker prepares drafts every 15 seconds, using historical closing balances and current unreserved funds. IPFS schedule checkpoints are retained independently of playlist/payment snapshots. Defaults in `payroll-assets.json.radioPayflow`: 100% unreserved budget, 0.01 USDC minimum, 1 USDC average-share warning. It never signs payouts. Historical RPC or backup failure stops preparation; after downtime, older eligible periods are processed first. Use `calendar=new-york` on `/api/radio/history` for the new buckets; default UTC history is preserved.

### NFT Artwork Defaults

Discord NFT requests and `/jukebox submit` default to the submitting user's pinned Discord profile image, including an animated avatar when available. Existing custom artwork is preserved. Missing profile defaults on pending Discord requests are recovered when the private Admin queue is read. The Discord modal cannot prefill its native file upload with an existing avatar; the optional upload/CID fields replace the default, and the confirmation shows the selected image.

Admin previews the queued image and supports PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF uploads up to 10 MB or an existing image/GIF file CID with no upload-size cap. Choose one replacement source, not both. `/api/ipfs/artwork-cid` validates/normalizes a file CID; it does not fetch/pin the entire image or guarantee its availability/type. Larger GIFs may render slowly depending on gateway/browser resources. A website-only submission does not establish a Discord identity.

### Payment Proof Service

`GET /api/payroll/ledger` exposes verified Base payments and IPFS snapshot status. Allowed browser origins can submit a transaction hash to `POST /api/payroll/reconcile`; the worker accepts only successful, canonical, twice-confirmed `PayrollPaid` events from the configured router and DecentBusking repository namespace. No signing key is held by the bot. A 15-second comparator discovers new events, rechecks saved proofs and retries pending backups. Tagged payment snapshots are retained independently of playlist snapshots. Radio state advertises this endpoint for DJuke/DBusk consumers.

Optional server variables: `PAYROLL_START_BLOCK` specifies historical scan coverage (default: startup head minus 2,000 unless restoring); `PAYROLL_ARCHIVE_RPC_URL` selects an archive-capable Base endpoint for weekly closing-balance checks (defaults to `https://mainnet.base.org`); `JUKELOOP_PAYROLL_RECOVERY_CID` accepts a comma-separated list overriding the one-time archived playlist checkpoints used to recover weekly counters; `PINATA_GATEWAY_TOKEN` is a server-only access key for a restricted Pinata gateway; `PAYROLL_GITHUB_TOKEN` is an owner credential with Actions-write permission for automatic dispatch of verified repo-dev ledger updates. Never put credentials in browser configuration. Without `PAYROLL_GITHUB_TOKEN`, the GitHub ledger workflow remains manual. See [payroll procedures](../docs/PAYROLL.md) for confirmation, backup, history and batch limitations.

### Setting up JukeLoop

1. Create a `JukeLoop` voice channel and a `JukeLoop` text channel in your server.
2. Copy both channel IDs (Developer Mode → right-click → Copy Channel ID).
3. Add to `.env`:
   ```
   JUKE_LOOP_VOICE_CHANNEL_ID=<voice-channel-id>
   JUKE_LOOP_TEXT_CHANNEL_ID=<text-channel-id>
   ```
4. Restart the bot — it will backfill existing tracks automatically.

## Upload → IPFS Pin Flow

```
User posts audio in #DecentJukebox
    ↓
Bot detects message attachments with audio MIME type or extension
    ↓
Track is immediately added to the JukeLoop playlist (if JukeLoop is enabled)
    ↓
Bot downloads the file buffer via fetch
    ↓
Bot uploads through Pinata or local Kubo → receives CID
    ↓
Bot builds mint URL:
  https://thejollylama.github.io/DecentBusking/?title=<track>&ipfs=<CID>
    ↓
Bot replies with a rich embed containing the "🎸 Mint This As A DNFT" link

```

Supported audio formats: `mp3`, `wav`, `ogg`, `flac`, `m4a`, `aac`, `opus`, `weba`

## Discord Developer Portal Setup

1. Go to [https://discord.com/developers/applications](https://discord.com/developers/applications) and create a new application.
2. Under **Bot**, click *Add Bot* and copy the **Token** → `DISCORD_TOKEN`.
3. Under **Bot → Privileged Gateway Intents**, enable **Message Content Intent**.
   (Voice channel support uses the non-privileged `GuildVoiceStates` intent — no extra toggle needed.)
4. Under **OAuth2 → URL Generator**, select scopes:
   - `bot`
   - `applications.commands`
   
   And permissions:
   - `Send Messages`
   - `Read Message History`
   - `Embed Links`
   - `Connect` (voice)
   - `Speak` (voice)
5. Use the generated URL to invite the bot to your server.
6. Enable Discord **Developer Mode** (Settings → Advanced), right-click `#jukebox`, and choose **Copy Channel ID** → `JUKEBOX_CHANNEL_ID`.

> **Note:** Global slash commands can take up to 1 hour to propagate after first registration. For faster iteration during development, register commands to a specific guild by replacing `Routes.applicationCommands(clientId)` with `Routes.applicationGuildCommands(clientId, guildId)` in `index.js` — guild commands update instantly.

## Deployment (Railway — recommended)

1. Push this repository to GitHub.
2. Create a new [Railway](https://railway.app) project and connect the repo.
3. Set the **Root Directory** to `discord-bot`.
4. Add the environment variables in the Railway dashboard under *Variables*.
5. Add a `NIXPACKS_PKGS=ffmpeg` variable so Railway installs FFmpeg automatically.
6. Railway will run `npm start` automatically.

### Alternative: fly.io

```bash
cd discord-bot

fly launch --name decentbusking-jukebox-bot
fly secrets set DISCORD_TOKEN=... JUKEBOX_CHANNEL_ID=... PINATA_JWT=... MINT_OWNER_WALLET=...
fly deploy
```

Add `ffmpeg` to your `Dockerfile` or `fly.toml` build configuration.

### Alternative: PM2 on a VPS

```bash
# Install FFmpeg first
sudo apt install ffmpeg

npm install -g pm2
pm2 start index.js --name jukebox-bot
pm2 save && pm2 startup
```

# Named DJuke playlists — rollout decisions

Queue-selection timeouts are scheduling deferrals, not playback failures. A
slow durable reservation remains in flight and is retained for the next selection
instead of repeatedly releasing and recreating its checkpoint. Before playback,
the worker revalidates its recording, pending status, and main-request priority.
Unheard selections discarded for a scheduled handoff or priority change are
released back to pending without refunding or settling the batch.
Permanently unavailable recordings and exhausted media retries still use
the refund safety net. A successful purchase is not evidence that the entire
playlist played; confirm delivery and refund events before reporting completion.

Paid playlists use the public radio's existing player, next-resource prefetcher,
changeover gap and priority checks, not a separate per-song payment/player loop.
The confirmed queue snapshot includes up to 24 consecutive playlist lane slots
(one maximum-sized playlist window). The next purchased song can be reserved
and prepared while the current song plays. Preparing it does not create a purchase
or settle its payment. It may start only after every preceding pending lane in the
window has a durable `played` or `fulfilled` journal record. A new main paid request,
refund, replacement or protected show still invalidates a prepared selection.

Settlement is single-flight and runs independently of playback selection. A slow
transaction no longer blocks preparation or the next song once clean playback
evidence is durable. Contract fulfillment remains head-only and ordered. A suffix
refund waits until preceding delivered songs have settled, so it cannot refund
their already-heard playback. The same guard applies when the next recording is

unplayable or missing locally, not just when media retries are exhausted.
Completed but unsettled journal records are not
replayed on restart.

Before decoding a paid playlist recording, the worker downloads its entire source
into a temporary local file. This avoids holding a backpressured HTTP connection
open for the duration of a song (or while its decoder is prefetched), which exposed
playback to gateway disconnects and repeated partial plays. Transfers have a
90-second deadline, a 256 MiB limit, and checks for empty/partial HTTP responses and
declared length mismatches. Failed downloads never start audio. Shutdown cancels
downloads; decoder closure removes each temporary file. Clean decoder EOF and
full PCM consumption are still required; buffering does not label damaged media
as delivered.

The standalone radio widget also preloads the published next source using the
same bounded blob downloader as the main website (80 MiB browser limit). It
finishes the current recording before handing off, consumes the prepared blob,
and will not restart an ended play ID just because polling repeats that state.
Preloads are cancelled on pause, station change, failure or destruction and are
disabled on data-saver/2G connections. An unavailable preload is logged and the
normal source remains available; it does not count as a paid delivery failure.

Failed journal completion, release and media-failure writes are retained in the
runtime and retried before queue selection and playback authorization. A transient
mirror failure therefore cannot strand a `playing` reservation after its radio
session loses the local reference, or replay an already-completed song merely
because its checkpoint needs retrying. Validation failures are not retained as

retryable writes. A process crash before evidence becomes durable still cannot
prove delivery; the existing conservative restart behavior remains.

While a known paid playlist remains unfinished, ordinary rotation is held rather
than starting unrelated music. The hold uses the verified remaining-lane count as
well as the journal; stale prefetched rotation is discarded at the handoff.
Status shows preparation/retry state and elapsed idle time, becoming recovering
when the existing watchdog threshold is exceeded instead of claiming preparation
indefinitely. The website distinguishes an incomplete-playback retry from preparing
the next song, and explicitly labels a paid hold longer than 30 seconds as delayed.
Slow durable storage or failed media can still introduce gaps;
this is not a promise of gapless streaming under failures.
Main paid requests, eligible advert breaks, and protected scheduled/live shows
retain their existing priority. Once the final paid delivery settles, ordinary
rotation resumes. A controlled worker shutdown releases reservations without
refunding the remaining batch.

Transient playlist media lookup errors, preparation timeouts, and interrupted or
insufficiently audible playback receive **three retries after the initial attempt**
before refunding the remaining batch (four failed media attempts total). Retry
counters are per song and durably stored in the playback journal, so restarts do
not reset the budget. Scheduling deferrals and slow checkpoint selection do not
consume it. Preparation retries back off for 5, 10, then 20 seconds and keep
ordinary rotation held; radio status explains the retry without requesting a new
payment. A partial recording is not settled as delivered, even if it ran for more

than 30 seconds. The fourth media failure invokes the existing version-specific
suffix/fee refund; v0.4 refunds the full reserved platform fee, not worker ETH or
wallet network gas. Refunds already completed are final and are not requeued.

### Verified audio completion (#274)

Paid delivery is no longer inferred from a mutable session-wide FFmpeg exit code
at the instant the player becomes Idle. Each prepared resource owns a PCM byte
counter and decoder lifecycle monitor. A clean completion requires consumed source
EOF, a successful matching decoder exit with no stream error or termination signal,
and consumption of all decoded PCM (within one 20 ms encoding frame). An EOF that
arrives just before the process exit notification waits at most one second for that
exit; missing evidence remains a failure, never an assumed delivery.
FFmpeg stops on decode errors instead of silently returning success for damaged
packets. Early player stops, incomplete streams and unconsumed decoded audio cannot
settle a playlist song. Scheduled handoffs and controlled shutdowns release a
reservation without spending its media retry budget. After four media failures,
recovery retries the suffix refund, not a fifth playback attempt, including after
a failed refund or restart.

Completion logs identify the play, track, paid request/attempt and decoder PID,
exit code/signal, source EOF/error, decoded PCM bytes/duration, consumed duration
and wall-clock audible time. Decoder stderr is drained but retained only as bounded
network/decode/timing categories and a byte count; raw media URLs or credentials
are not included. Playback checkpoint, settlement and deferred-selection timings
make bookkeeping gaps distinguishable from audio failures. Duration evidence is

decoded PCM, not an assumed trustworthy duration from a gateway response.

Profile → Playlists receipts include the failed song, sanitized failure category,
failed-attempt count and exhausted-retry status alongside the existing exact
on-chain delivered/refunded amounts. An already-refunded purchase is final; the
repair does not replay or recharge it.

The regression in `test/playlist-audio-completion.test.js` drives twelve actual
HTTP download → local FFmpeg → PCM → Opus → player → Idle completions through the
paid journal/runtime and the normal radio prefetcher. It blocks settlement until
all twelve songs have played and fails the fifth song's first completion checkpoint.
It checks twelve starts/deliveries exactly once and in order, one source download
per song, no refund, and transitions below two seconds with the intentional
2.5-second radio changeover sleep stubbed out. It does not inject successful audio
completion verdicts or establish production latency under slow durable storage.
Separate tests cover broken/oversized/timed-out downloads, retryable checkpoint
failures, main-request priority and safe suffix refunds.
A real player regression severs a preload's first HTTP transfer, verifies that no
partial audio starts, retains one preparation failure and its retry backoff, then
completes and settles the retried recording exactly once without a refund.
By default the playback regression uses short local WAV fixtures served over HTTP.
To repeat the incident-media check, download the
public CID `bafybeicgdqwqww2frcnmvjmitt5zvqivtg3vemyekr7johxlkkdllea4di`
and run:

```sh
DJUKE_INCIDENT_MEDIA=/path/to/recording.m4a node --test \
  --test-name-pattern='twelve real player EOFs' test/playlist-audio-completion.test.js
```

The file is served locally with byte-range support (required for seekable M4A)
and occupies the fifth slot. The October 24 check completed all twelve once, in
order, without a refund: the incident recording decoded 32,149,248 PCM bytes
(167,444 ms) and the player consumed 167,440 ms, within its 20 ms frame boundary.
This verifies the actual recording/player lifecycle, not a new production payment.
Successful local decoding does not identify the original gateway/network failure.
The latest production diagnostics below distinguish incomplete source consumption
from a successful EOF that only needs to wait for a decoder exit notification.

### October 25 monitored batch and seamless-transition fixes (#284)

BoogieNight batch 2 on v0.5 (lanes 24–35) ran with the continuity changes above
deployed. All twelve songs played and were delivered with no repeats, media
failures or refunds; lane 30, the source that ended batch 1, played cleanly. It
settled in `0x94b4b2e6e4ff585807c5ed0f5c13d6ad930184fe5087e68ab7313b6a2f2f9fa0`.
Transitions were still not radio-like: about 8 s at best and up to 79 s at worst,
with these causes:

- Every journal commit waited for the local checkpoint mirror. Required DJuke
  journals shared a two-job queue with best-effort radio, hype and show mirrors, so
  `Checkpoint mirror queue is full` rejected required commits (31→32, 34→35),
  disposed the prefetched song and forced a fresh selection. The local client also

polled only every 5 seconds.
- A paid selection that took longer than its 10-second limit returned `null` to the
  prefetcher, which did not try again before the current song ended (25→26 took
  four timeouts).
- The handoff waited for the finished song's durable `played` checkpoint before the
  next lane could start, even after clean audio evidence existed.
- After more than 30 seconds of silence the browser treated the next song as a
  fresh join and started it at the live position, so listeners missed its first
  10–20 seconds. The embeddable widget always started at the live position.
- The queue card counted only on-chain `delivered` events, which arrive after
  settlement, so it showed "6 of 12 remaining" while song 8 played. The radio badge
  used a remaining count saved at reservation time.

Fixes:

- The mirror queue gives required journals their own capacity of 8, separate from
  16 best-effort jobs, and offers them first. A newer best-effort snapshot of a
  store replaces its unclaimed predecessor. Idle claims long-poll for up to
  10 seconds, and the client claims again immediately after each job.
- The prefetcher retries a `null` paid-playlist selection with 1–5 second backoff
  while the current song plays.
- Clean, finished audio from the previous lane is in-memory evidence that lets the
  next lane pass `canPlay` while the `played` checkpoint is stored. Settlement and
  refunds still require the durable record. Incomplete audio and media retries
  still block the next lane. A crash before the checkpoint replays the lane.
- A listener whose song ended keeps polling quickly for up to 5 minutes while the
  server is between songs, then starts the next song from 0:00 if it is within
  45 seconds of the start. The widget follows the same rule.

- Each lane carries its `position` in the batch. The radio badge shows "Song N of
  M". Open batches mark the live lane `playing`, and lanes with clean audio or a
  durable played record are marked `played`. The queue card shows
  "Song N of M · R remaining", and receipts show played songs that are still
  settling.
- The standalone DJuke widget (`widget-djuke.html`) uses the same
  `js/djuke-playlist-progress.mjs` helper as the drawer for its queue and receipts.
  The DBusk radio widget (`widget.html`) applies the same 0:00 handoff. The
  standalone DVert controllers get playback from their host, and on the main site
  they share the single versioned `radio-sync.js` instance.

known-address book as **DJuke v0.5** and **DJuke v0.4** (with v0.3 retained),
linking to their BaseScan contract pages rather than showing an unnamed wallet.

are authorized by the funding policy. The connected admin sees worker funding

The optional automatic reserve remains disabled and outside the selected launch

The public catalog never waits for reconciliation or checkpoint writes. Its
read-only batch snapshot supplies the complete ordered queue; exact, uniquely

Radio takeover badges and bounded, slow 3D notes/balloons/genies appear only

Issue #241 adds a profile-backed playlist library. Names are 1–60 characters;

wallets pin the exact revision and ordered song IDs, never a moving pointer.
Only the maker can publish a new revision. A saved copy preserves maker, ID,

### Guided playlist tutorial

follows the bunny; reduced motion skips the travel and decorative flow animation.
The same card appears in the general tour after the DJuke introduction.

The guide opens only the drawer and playlist disclosure. It never edits the draft,

illustrations, not live transactions or fabricated station state. Closing early
restores the prior disclosure/drawer state; finishing the linked guide leaves
DJuke open without marking the whole site tour complete. No Discord announcement

The draft exposes exactly three actions: **Save to Profile** signs and stores a

named revision without buying playback; **Personal Play** buys the current ordered
draft in one creator-priced batch, then plays all songs consecutively locally;
**Play Live** buys the draft for the shared radio playlist lane. Saving is optional
for either playback purchase. Personal Play does not affect public radio and has
no radio platform fee. Play Live preserves the tier prices and main paid-request
priority below; it never interrupts a song already playing. Both purchases may
need a separate USDC approval, and wallet gas is additional.

### Protected shows and conditional Play Live warnings

Play Live buys queued delivery, **not an uninterrupted or guaranteed-time radio
slot**. Protected radio hours and scheduled shows take priority. A mix can wait or
be set aside for a protected block; its remaining songs return to the queue after
the block ends without a second payment. Main paid requests can still cut in
between songs. A scheduling delay or interruption alone does **not** trigger a
refund. This does not remove the separate failed-delivery refund policy below.

The general terms are in DJuke's **i** information, the linked bunny tutorial, and
the standalone widget's **How DJuke works** disclosure. There is **no blanket
confirmation window** on ordinary Play Live checkout.

Before network switching, gas quoting, USDC approval, or purchase, the shared
`checkoutRadioPlaylist` helper reads fresh public calendar, queue, and radio
snapshots. It uses `radioCalendarOccurrences` (the public calendar's own New York
weekly/DST expansion) to compare protected blocks with an estimated window from
now through current/queued audio plus the purchased playlist. Known durations
use `durationMs` or `durationSeconds`; unknown songs use a clearly disclosed rough

**four-minute-per-song** allowance. Pending counts cover playlist lanes omitted
from the bounded queue window. A currently audible DJuke request is counted only
once when its public request ID also appears in the pending queue.

**Only a detected overlap** opens a pre-purchase message naming the dated show and
New York start/end times, playlist and wait estimates, approximation caveats, and
the scheduling/refund terms. Cancel stops checkout and leaves the draft
unchanged. Acknowledging continues normal wallet checkout. The check runs for
unsaved drafts, saved/profile mixes, and the standalone widget, but not for
Personal Play or saving. No acknowledgment is remembered for later purchases.
Unavailable calendar/queue data or invalid times stop checkout with an explicit
retry error rather than silently claiming no conflict. These estimates cannot
predict new requests, ad breaks, media retries, schedule changes, or exact
start/finish times; no detected overlap is not an uninterrupted-play guarantee.

Reuse: adapt the shared checkout from `bac5caa` and the public calendar occurrence
helper, rather than duplicating calendar logic or payment handlers.
The existing radio handoff releases paid reservations rather than treating a
protected-show interruption as a failed delivery.

### Personal Play recovery

New Personal Play purchases retain a wallet-scoped session in this browser's
local storage: the submitted Base transaction hash, receiving contract, ordered
recordings, current song, and playback position. The transaction is saved before
waiting for its confirmation, so a refresh during confirmation can be recovered
too. Storage is checked before checkout; an unfinished purchase of the same
ordered songs blocks accidental duplicate payment.

After a refresh or media interruption, open **Profile → Playlists → Your Personal
Play sessions** and choose **Resume · no payment** (or **Resume / retry** during
an active session). Resume verifies the original transaction on Base, including
the purchasing wallet, destination, and successful receipt, without approval or
another purchase. A pending transaction remains recoverable; a verified reverted
transaction is marked failed. Playback resumes the current song near the last
saved position and continues the remaining songs in order. Progress saves every
second, on pause/seek, page hide, and visibility changes; loading must not overwrite
a saved position with zero. A gateway/media failure does not complete the session.
Completion is recorded only after the final song ends.

Recovery requires the same browser/site storage and purchasing wallet. It is not
cross-device, does not auto-start audio after refresh, and cannot recover older
purchases made before sessions were stored or sessions erased by clearing site
data. Session storage is not an on-chain playback entitlement. It does not change
personal-listen settlement or create an automatic refund for media failures.
The public radio keeps running for other listeners throughout personal playback.

Private checkout sums each song's normal creator/album listen price (0.25 USDC
default), with no platform fee and no radio request. Radio subtotal is the sum of
`250000 << floor(i / 8)` USDC base units for zero-based playlist index i: songs
1–8 cost $0.25 each, 9–16 $0.50 each, 17–24 $1 each. Radio platform fee is
**$3 × ceil(n / 12)**, split equally 25/25/25/25 across Playback, Top10, Pinners,
and Repo funds (rounding remainder to Repo). Examples: 8 songs $2 + $3; 12 songs

$4 + $3; 24 songs $14 + $6 = **$20**. Pricing is independent of queue depth.
The UI mirrors this formula for display and prefers on-chain `quotePlaylist`
when a configured contract and provider are available; checkout always quotes
on-chain (radio via the signed worker endpoint). Private creator prices may differ
from the local default estimate.

Each delivered radio song settles 90% directly to artists/collaborators, 8% to
pinners, and 2% to Repo, separately from the platform fee. The entire platform fee
is reserved until every song is delivered, then settled once to the four funds.
`refundUndeliveredPlaylist(batchId)` refunds pending song amounts and the entire
reserved fee; delivered songs retain their settlement. Refunded lane items advance
the lane head rather than blocking later batches. Durable events track
`PlaylistBatchRequested(..., firstLaneId)`, `PlaylistSongDelivered`,
`PlaylistSongRefunded`, `PlaylistBatchFeeSettled`, and `PlaylistBatchFeeRefunded`.
Lane journals use schema 2; old FIFO-batch schema 1 must not be silently replayed
as lane IDs. UI/worker must use confirmed events, never transaction submission,
for settled/refunded state.

Worker gas remains separate: the EIP-712 `PlaylistGasQuote` uses domain
DecentJukeBox / 0.2 and binds listener, ordered-song hash, max total, per-song
fulfillment cost, nonce, and deadline. Checkout forwards exactly
`fulfillmentCostWei * 2 * n` native ETH to the gas worker immediately. This is
not refunded by a later USDC batch refund. The endpoint sizes a
`fulfillPlaylistSong` transaction, returns on-chain subtotal/fee, and accepts
1–24 distinct songs. The UI shows this full contribution before confirmation;
initial USDC allowance may require a separate approval.

## Playback and scheduling

Radio playlists occupy a **separate playlist lane**, never the main paid FIFO.
Normal paid requests always cut in before pending playlist songs. The worker reads
main requests first and `playlistHeadId` / `playlistNextId` / `getPlaylistItem` at
the same confirmed block. It claims only the playlist lane head when main pending
is zero, and calls `fulfillPlaylistSong(laneId, expectedSongId, expectedRevision,
playbackProof)` only after audible completion. Lane recordings are immutable
(expected revision 0). If a main request arrives during playback, settlement waits
until the main queue clears; proof is retained durably, not discarded or replayed.
The contract independently enforces the same cut-in rule. Refund recovery calls
`refundUndeliveredPlaylist(batchId)`, not a main-request refund. Main request IDs
and playlist lane IDs have distinct durable journal identities. `pendingCount`
remains main-only; main quote tiering uses main + playlist pending. This does not
interrupt current audio or preempt protected Top 10, live, or scheduled shows;
existing DVert break policy remains unchanged.

## DJuke contract and policy gates

Published JollyJukeBox mappings distinguish Polygon v1.2 from Optimism
v1.2.4-v1.2.6. The v1.2.5 and v1.2.6 ABIs accept multiple album owners;
they do not expose retroactive artist editing or weighted share parameters.
ABI evidence alone does not establish actual distribution or refund behavior.
Verify the relevant Solidity sources before reusing those mechanisms.

Keep payment receipts and queue fulfillment separate from NFT ownership.
Queue requests must bind payment to the canonical song, resist replay, and

only become eligible after payment verification. Do not interrupt the current
song. The user's no-refund direction requires durable paid requests, restart
recovery, pre-payment availability checks and retries after playback failures.
Do not silently expire or discard paid requests, or equate a payment event with
completed playback. Escalating prices discourage long queues but do not
guarantee content availability or a fulfillment deadline.

Approved pricing (2026-10-10, supersedes the initial $1 price): the starting
price is 0.25 USDC and doubles for each eight pending paid requests. Count
the queue before adding the new request: 0-7 costs 0.25, 8-15 costs 0.50,
16-23 costs 1.00, 24-31 costs 2.00, and so on. As the pending count falls, so
does the next request price. Every price allocates 8% to the pinners fund,
2% to repo-dev, and 90% to the song's artist, including approved collaborators.
Verify the existing fund's on-chain identifier and deposit route before wiring
this allocation; do not substitute an assumed wallet address.

Native Base USDC is the approved payment asset. At its six decimals, the
starting price is 250,000 units: 20,000 for pinners, 5,000 for repo-dev, and
225,000 for the artist/collaborators. Keep fractional-cent splits exact. The payment contract
must compute the authoritative quote at acceptance and reject a price above
the user's approved maximum; a changed queue must never cause a surprise
charge. Client-side prices are informational, not transaction authority.

The local DJuke right-side drawer now shows the tier model, a queue display,
song selection and a shared-wallet connection control. It polls the gated
`GET /api/djuke` endpoint; the payment contract candidate is not deployed.

The response supplies ordered `requests` (unique `requestId`,
`trackId`, `title`, optional `artist`) and available `tracks` (`trackId`,
`title`). Unavailable or invalid responses clear the quote rather than showing
a false empty queue. The payment button remains disabled in all states.
No USDC approval, payment or queue submission is implemented or enabled.
Desktop/mobile browser checks use mocked queue and wallet state.

First-paid, first-played remains the proposed queue order. Paid plays count
toward weekly qualification; permanently unavailable recordings allow a
payer-chosen replacement. Collaborative shares also need consent and rules for

## Agreed policy

- Native USDC on Base. Anyone may request an active, approved campaign.
- Base queue price: $1 times `2 ** floor(pendingCount / 7)`, counting both tiers.
  A **queue bump** costs that quote and replaces the first available slot at a
  normally scheduled main-radio advert break, without adding another break.
  A displaced ordinary advert remains eligible for subsequent rotation.
- **Play after this song** costs exactly **2x the current queue price** and buys
  an extra break after the current recording. It preserves ordinary advert
  reservations and does not reset the normal-break cadence.
- Immediate requests take priority over bumps; each tier remains FIFO. A new
  immediate request can preempt a bump being prepared, but never interrupt
  audio already playing. Multiple immediate requests wait in FIFO order.
  Both tiers defer throughout protected Top 10/live programming.
- At most 128 outstanding queue positions; the ID scan window is also bounded
  to 128, so an old pending bump can temporarily fill the window even if later
  immediate requests settle. Checkout approves only the current exact tier
  price; the contract enforces the payer's maximum price.
- Purchased title, advertiser and media URI are immutable request snapshots.
  Campaign expiry does not invalidate a purchased play.

- USDC remains reserved in the queue until the radio fulfiller reports a
  naturally finished audible play. Then 45% goes to Top 10, 45% playback, 8%
  pinners and 2% repo development through the existing router.
- Removed campaigns leave the playable queue. Only each original payer can
  claim their full unplayed request payment. Refunds work while paused.
  No general admin withdrawal is available.

## Trust and failure behavior

The fulfiller is trusted to attest radio playback, approve catalog-matched
campaigns, and mirror authorized campaign removals on-chain. An on-chain
transaction cannot independently prove Discord audio delivery. This follows
DJuke's worker-attestation model; it is not trustless proof of listening.
Approval matches the existing verified NFT/advert catalog before the worker
marks a campaign queueable.

The worker checkpoints reservation and completed playback to Pinata and the
checkpoint mirror before settling. A unique proof and on-chain FIFO head
prevent duplicate/out-of-order settlement. Failed fetches, interruption,
reverted settlement, or worker restart do not release the payment. A lost
playback checkpoint can result in replay, not a second charge.

The paid-ad journal explicitly requires local mirroring before publishing each
checkpoint. If the mirror is offline, fails to pin, or returns a different CID,
the journal save fails and the paid request does not advance. Other existing
checkpoint stores retain their normal best-effort community mirror behavior.
Run `node checkpoint-mirror-client.js --watch` from `discord-bot` on the operator
Mac, with IPFS Desktop running and the same `CHECKPOINT_MIRROR_SECRET` as Render.
The helper accepts playlist checkpoints and validated paid-playback journals.

It must remain running for paid-ad playback and settlement.
The replacement journal's filename and metadata kind include its contract
address, so request #0 from the new deployment cannot reuse the old journal.

Removal is cross-system: the durable campaign-removal ledger is updated first,
then the queue contract is reconciled. Failure is reported rather than showing
a completed refund. The worker blocks new starts for the campaign and defers
on-chain removal while its paid request is playing or has finished but is not
yet settled. Interrupted playback returns to the queue; naturally completed
playback is settled before removal can make an unplayed request refundable.
Periodic reconciliation retries even during protected shows. Payers must wait
for confirmed on-chain removal to claim.

There is no automatic timeout refund for a stalled worker: paid plays survive
campaign expiry by agreement. Admin must remove a campaign to authorize
unplayed refunds if service cannot be delivered. Worker gas is operator-funded
in this version; there is no extra ETH contribution charged to buyers.

# Your First Visit To DecentBusking

Start here: [open DecentBusking](https://thejollylama.github.io/DecentBusking/). You can listen and explore without connecting a wallet. Take the listener route first; submit a song only when you are ready to share it publicly.

## Follow The White Rabbit

Look for **Follow the white rabbit** in the center of the landing scene. The large
**☿** Mercury symbol follows the rabbit with a small flying-money icon and
different musical accessories at every stop. Mercury is a visual companion,
not a narrator. A white rabbit peeks out of little rabbit holes beside each
stop, with factual text explaining the controls. The tour opens the actual
briefcase, Top 10, DVert, DJuke, archive, and both ankh menus, explaining what each
is for without voting, submitting, connecting a wallet, paying, or starting audio.

Choose **Follow**, **Back**, or **Leave tour** at your own pace. Arrow keys move
between stops when the card has focus; Tab also lets you explore the page. On exit,
previously open drawers and any visible briefcase draft are restored. Finish any
pending submission, close other dialogs, and return from VertLoop to main radio
before starting. Reduced-motion settings keep the rabbit and Mercury still.
The card count sits beside **Follow the White Rabbit**. A centered hole in the
card is the rabbit's home: it dives down, emerges beside the highlighted feature
with a short hop and sparkles, and returns home before the next card appears.
Navigation pauses briefly during the trip; **Leave tour** and **Close tutorial**
remain available. Outside clicks and Escape do not dismiss the tour.
Reduced motion skips the trip and decorative effects.
After completing every stop, the landing-page button is hidden in that browser.

Leaving early does not count as completion. Click **DBusker** to open **About**
and use the identical **Follow the white rabbit** button to replay the tour.
Music notes and little sound-wave rings accompany Mercury's arrivals. These are
visual effects, not extra audio over the radio.

### Build a DJuke playlist with the bunny

[Open the playlist tutorial](https://thejollylama.github.io/DecentBusking/?tutorial=playlists).
This link opens directly to the playlist card even if you have already completed
the general tour. The same card is included after DJuke in the full walkthrough.
Mercury follows the bunny between the real controls:

1. Search for a song or creator and choose a song.
2. Use **Add selected song** to build a draft of up to 24 songs.
3. Name the mix, reorder with **↑ / ↓**, or remove a song with **×**.
4. **Save to Profile** signs and keeps a named revision, without buying playback.
5. **Personal Play** buys your mix at creator prices for your ears only.
6. **Play Live** queues it for the community, at the displayed radio tier prices
   plus $3 per started group of 12 songs. Base network gas is additional.
   Protected hours/shows can set your mix aside; remaining songs return to the
   queue afterward without another payment.
   There is no refund solely for that delay or interruption. Separate
   failed-delivery refunds still apply; exact playback times are not guaranteed.
   If your estimated playlist/current/queued playback overlaps a protected block
   on the public calendar, checkout names the show and asks before proceeding.
   Unknown song lengths use a rough four-minute-per-song allowance; ordinary
   checkout without a detected overlap has no separate confirmation window.

7. See how song payments split 90% to musicians/collaborators, 8% to pinning, and
   2% to development, while the separate radio fee splits 25% each to Playback,
